explanation: Folklorists find no link: the rhyme first appeared in print in 1881, and the plague reading arose in the 20th century. Early versions have no sneezing line.

claims.text: There is no evidence that the nursery rhyme 'Ring a Ring o' Roses' is about the plague.
The rhyme first appeared in print in 1881, in Kate Greenaway's Mother Goose.
The idea that the rhyme describes the plague arose in the 20th century.
Early printed versions of the rhyme have no sneezing line.
Folklorists, among them Iona and Peter Opie, reject the plague interpretation.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: The search turned up a consistent picture: the Great Plague reading is a 20th-century folk belief that folklorists reject, and the 1881 Greenaway book is the earliest printed English appearance. Scholarly consensus: Folklore scholars consider the Great Plague explanation of the rhyme to be unfounded for several reasons. The plague explanation did not emerge until the mid-twentieth century.

claimResults.note: Wikipedia and the Library of Congress's American Folklife Center: folklore scholars consider the plague explanation unfounded. This external evidence also clears the ring-a-roses-plague myth hit, which both checks confirmed directly.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Greenaway (1881): Most sources treat Kate Greenaway's Mother Goose as the first printed appearance in English. One says the first publication of "Ring Around the Rosie" in English was that 1881 book. Pre-1881 material: Wikipedia cites an American variant recorded as being used in Connecticut in the 1840s and an 1855 novel containing a version. Conflicting claim: A Wikipedia "Nursery rhyme" table says the earliest recorded version of the rhyme appears in Thomas d'Urfey's play The Campaigners from 1698. The other sources don't support this.

claimResults.note: The sources conflict on 'first appeared in print in 1881': the Library of Congress blog calls Greenaway's 1881 book the first publication in English, but Wikipedia cites a version in an 1855 novel and a Connecticut variant from the 1840s, and search 15 says Wikipedia calls Greenaway 'another early record'. A conflict fails the claim as written (guide 9.5.2).

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Plague link arrived late: Interpreters of the rhyme before World War II make no mention of this connection. In 1951, the first direct reference to the plague interpretation appears, when Iona and Peter Opie note that some people believe the rhyme refers to the plague, but they are not convinced. Scholarly consensus: Folklore scholars consider the Great Plague explanation of the rhyme to be unfounded for several reasons. The plague explanation did not emerge until the mid-twentieth century.

claimResults.note: The first direct reference to the plague reading is the Opies' in 1951, and interpreters before the Second World War never mention it.

claimResults.note: An early printed version has the sneeze: Wikipedia quotes the 1883 Shropshire folklore collection with a sneezing refrain ('they stand and imitate sneezing'), and search 15 says the same of the Shropshire version. So 'early printed versions have no sneezing line' is false as a general statement, whatever the 1881 text says.

Keep what the sources agree on, for example 'Folklorists find no link: the plague reading appeared only in the mid-20th century, and earlier interpreters never mention it.'
